text: Magdalena Carmen Frida Kahlo y Calderón (Spanish pronunciation: [ˈfɾiða ˈkalo]; 6 July 1907 – 13 July 1954) was a Mexican painter renowned for her portraits, self-portraits, and works inspired by nature and Mexican artifacts. Influenced by the country’s popular culture, she used a naïve folk art style to explore themes of identity, postcolonialism, gender, class, and race in Mexican society. Her paintings often had strong autobiographical elements and blended realism with fantasy. Associated with the post-revolutionary Mexicayotl movement, Kahlo has also been described as a surrealist or magical realist and is known for depicting her chronic pain. Her 1940 self-portrait, The Dream (The Bed), holds the record as the most expensive work by a female artist ever auctioned, selling for $54.7 million. Born to a German father and a mestiza mother of Purépecha descent, Kahlo lived most of her life at La Casa Azul in Coyoacán, now the Frida Kahlo Museum. Though disabled by polio as a child, she was a promising medical student until a severe bus accident at 18 caused lifelong pain and medical issues. During recovery, she returned to art, initially considering a career as a medical illustrator. Her mother provided her with a specially-made easel and oil paints from her father, and a mirror was placed above the easel so she could see herself. Painting became a means to explore identity and existence, as she stated, "I paint myself because I am often alone and I am the subject I know best," and later, "to begin again, painting things just as [she] saw them with [her] own eyes and nothing more." Most of her early works were portraits of herself, her sisters, and schoolfriends, drawing inspiration from Renaissance artists like Botticelli and Bronzino and avant-garde movements such as Neue Sachlichkeit and Cubism. After moving to Cuernavaca in 1929 with Diego Rivera, she adopted a folk art style influenced by Adolfo Best Maugard’s treatise, incorporating elements from pre-Columbian and colonial Mexican art. In San Francisco in 1930, she met American artists like Edward Weston and Nickolas Muray, developed her folk art style, and created works such as Frieda and Diego Rivera (1931) and The Portrait of Luther Burbank (1931). Though she publicly presented herself as Rivera’s spouse, her work was included in the Sixth Annual Exhibition of the San Francisco Society of Women Artists. In Detroit, she faced health issues from a failed pregnancy and explored new techniques like etching and frescos, emphasizing themes of terror, suffering, wounds, and pain, and created retablo-style works such as Henry Ford Hospital (1932), My Birth (1932), and Self-Portrait on the Border of Mexico and the United States (1932). Despite no exhibitions in Detroit, she gave an interview to the Detroit News, titled "Wife of the Master Mural Painter Gleefully Dabbles in Works of Art." After returning to Mexico City in 1934, she made few paintings due to health issues, but in 1937 and 1938, following her divorce and reconciliation with Rivera, she produced more works than in all previous years, including My Nurse and I (1937), Memory, the Heart (1937), Four Inhabitants of Mexico (1938), and What the Water Gave Me (1938). The National Autonomous University of Mexico exhibited her work in early 1938, and she made her first significant sale in 1938 when Edward G. Robinson bought four paintings for $200 each. André Breton, impressed by her work, called it "a ribbon around a bomb," arranged her first solo exhibition at Julien Levy Gallery in New York in 1938, and later invited her to Paris in 1939. In New York, her colorful Mexican dress caused a sensation, and the exhibition, attended by Georgia O'Keeffe and Clare Boothe Luce, received positive press despite condescending reviews; she sold half of the 25 paintings. She received commissions from A. Conger Goodyear and Clare Boothe Luce. In Paris, despite Breton’s invitation, her paintings were not cleared by customs and the gallery refused to show most of them, considering them too shocking, and they were displayed alongside photographs, pre-Columbian sculptures, and Mexican market items. The exhibition opened in March 1939, received less attention due to the looming Second World War, and made a financial loss, leading her to cancel a planned London exhibition. However, the Louvre purchased The Frame, making her the first Mexican artist in their collection. She was warmly received by artists like Pablo Picasso and Joan Miró and by the fashion world, with Elsa Schiaparelli designing a dress inspired by her and Vogue Paris featuring her. Kahlo remained critical of the Surrealists, calling them "this bunch of coocoo lunatics and very stupid surrealists." In the United States, her work continued to gain attention, being featured at the Institute of Contemporary Art in Boston in 1941 and in two high-profile exhibitions in New York in 1942: the Twentieth-Century Portraits exhibition at MoMA and the Surrealists' First Papers of Surrealism exhibition. In 1943, she was included in the Mexican Art Today exhibition at the Philadelphia Museum of Art and Women Artists at Peggy Guggenheim's The Art of This Century gallery. In Mexico, she became a founding member of the Seminario de Cultura Mexicana in 1942, participated in exhibitions at the Benjamin Franklin Library in 1943 and 1944, and was invited to "Salon de la Flor." She also taught at the Escuela Nacional de Pintura, Escultura y Grabado ("La Esmeralda") starting in 1943, encouraging informal, non-hierarchical teaching and a focus on Mexican folk culture and street subjects. When her health prevented commuting, she held classes at La Casa Azul, and four students—Fanny Rabel, Arturo García Bustos, Guillermo Monroy, and Arturo Estrada—became devoted followers, known as "Los Fridos." She secured three mural commissions for herself and her students. Kahlo struggled to earn a living from her art until the mid to late 1940s, refusing to adapt her style, and received two government commissions in the early 1940s—one not completed and one rejected. However, she had regular private clients, such as engineer Eduardo Morillo Safa, who ordered over thirty family portraits. Her financial situation improved with a 5000-peso national prize for Moses (1945) in 1946 and the purchase of The Two Fridas by the Museo de Arte Moderno in 1947. By the mid-1940s, her paintings were featured in most group exhibitions in Mexico, and she could sell whatever she painted, sometimes incomplete works. As her health declined, she underwent a failed spinal surgery and painted works like Broken Column (1944), Moses (1945), Without Hope (1945), Tree of Hope, Stand Fast (1946), and The Wounded Deer (1946), reflecting her physical state. In her final years, she was mostly confined to La Casa Azul, painting still lifes of fruit and flowers with political symbols such as flags or doves. She expressed concern about expressing her political convictions, stating, "I have a great restlessness about my paintings... I must struggle with all my strength to ensure that the little positive my health allows me to do also benefits the Revolution, the only real reason to live." Her painting style became more intense, with brasher colors and faster brushstrokes. Photographer Lola Alvarez Bravo staged her first solo exhibition in Mexico at Galería Arte Contemporaneo in April 1953, despite her doctors’ bed rest orders; she arrived in an ambulance and was carried to the gallery, where she stayed for the event. The exhibition was a major cultural event and received global media attention. In 1954, Kahlo was hospitalized in April and May, then resumed painting after a one-year break, creating political works such as Marxism Will Give Health to the Sick (c. 1954), Frida and Stalin (c. 1954), and the still-life Viva La Vida (1954). Estimates vary on the total number of paintings she produced, ranging from fewer than 150 to around 200.

In 1953, despite her doctors prescribing bed rest, Frida Kahlo ordered her four-poster bed to be moved to the gallery for the opening of a major exhibition, which was a significant cultural event in Mexico and received international media attention. She arrived in an ambulance, was carried on a stretcher to the bed, and remained there throughout the event. That same year, the Tate Gallery in London held an exhibition on Mexican art that included five of her paintings. In 1954, Kahlo was hospitalized in April and May, after which she resumed painting following a one-year break. Her final works include the political paintings Marxism Will Give Health to the Sick (c. 1954) and Frida and Stalin (c. 1954), as well as the still-life Viva La Vida (1954). Estimates of her total output range from fewer than 150 to around 200 paintings. Her early works from the mid-1920s show influence from Renaissance masters and European avant-garde artists like Amedeo Modigliani, while by the end of the decade, she drew inspiration from Mexican folk art, particularly its themes of fantasy, naivety, and fascination with violence and death. Her style blended reality with surreal elements and frequently depicted pain and death. André Breton, a key early supporter, claimed her as a Surrealist, stating she developed her style without knowing the movement’s ideological foundations, and described her work as situated at the intersection of political and artistic lines. Bertram D. Wolfe called her a "sort of 'naïve' Surrealism," though Kahlo herself detested Surrealism, viewing it as bourgeois art. Some art historians, like Andrea Kettenmann, see her as a symbolist focused on inner experience, while Emma Dexter argues her work aligns more with magical realism or New Objectivity due to its roots in Aztec mythology and Mexican culture rather than Surrealism. Influenced by Mexicanidad, a romantic nationalism emerging after the revolution, Kahlo aimed to paint for the Mexican people and rejected the idea of formal art education, instead cultivating an image of being self-taught and naive. While muralists dominated the Mexican art scene in the 1920s, Kahlo focused on small-scale self-portraits, especially inspired by votive paintings or retablos—religious images made by amateurs to thank saints for surviving calamities—whose format emphasized figures over realistic backgrounds. She owned approximately 2,000 retablos, displayed in La Casa Azul, and used their narrative potential to explore allegory and iconography. Her self-portraits often mimicked colonial-era bust-length portraits but subverted them by portraying her as less attractive, reflecting shifting societal values in the 1930s as Mexicans moved away from socialism toward individualism. Her mask-like faces were linked to Indigenous and Catholic depictions of goddesses and saints. She was influenced by Mexican folk artists Hermenegildo Bustos and José Guadalupe Posada, as well as European artists Hieronymus Bosch and Pieter Bruegel the Elder, and poet Rosario Castellanos, whose works addressed female suffering and patriarchal structures. Root imagery in her paintings symbolizes personal growth, entrapment, and the influence of the past on the present; in My Grandparents and I, a young Kahlo holds a ribbon from an ancient tree bearing her ancestors’ portraits, with her left foot as a tree trunk, reflecting her view of humanity’s unity with the earth and Mexico. Trees represent hope, strength, and intergenerational continuity, while hair symbolizes growth and the feminine; in Self-Portrait with Cropped Hair, she wears a man’s suit and shorn hair, holding scissors menacingly near her genitals, interpreted as a threat to Rivera or a projection of her anger toward patriarchal values and machismo. Kahlo’s lifelong suffering from a youth bus accident led to frequent hospitalizations and surgeries, often performed by quacks, and her medical-themed paintings frequently depict bleeding and open wounds, especially in childbirth and miscarriage, reflecting guilt over living at the expense of others. Her paintings, though personal, are ambiguous and raise questions about Mexican society, particularly gender, race, and class. Historian Liza Bakewell notes Kahlo recognized the contradictions of being Mexican—modern yet pre-Columbian, young yet old, anti-Catholic yet Catholic, Western yet New World, independent yet colonized, mestizo yet not Spanish or Indian—and used pre-Columbian and Christian symbols, including monkeys, skeletons, skulls, blood, and hearts, often tied to Aztec myths like Coatlicue, Quetzalcoatl, and Xolotl. She also frequently depicted La Llorona and La Malinche, figures associated with suffering and misfortune, such as in Henry Ford Hospital (1932), where she painted herself weeping with an exposed heart, traditionally seen as a depiction of grief but now interpreted as a commentary on the taboo of remaining childless in Mexican society. Kahlo often portrayed her body in various states—wounded, as a child, or in different clothing like the Tehuana dress, a man’s suit, or a European gown—using it as a metaphor to explore societal roles. Her depictions of the female body, especially during miscarriages or childbirth and cross-dressing, position the viewer as a voyeur, making it difficult to avoid a conscious response. According to Nancy Cooey, Kahlo made herself into the central figure of her own mythology as a woman, a Mexican, and a suffering person, expressing spiritual resistance and sexuality. Nancy Deffebach notes she created a subject who was female, Mexican, modern, and powerful, diverging from traditional gender roles. Until the late 1980s, her work was often seen as less political and more naïve than that of male muralists. Art historian Joan Borsa criticizes that critical reception has frequently ignored or downplayed the politics in her exploration of personal history, including sexuality, marginality, cultural identity, female subjectivity, and power. Magdalena Carmen Frida Kahlo y Calderón was born on 6 July 1907 in Coyoacán, near Mexico City. While she claimed to have been born at La Casa Azul, the official registry lists the birth at her maternal grandmother’s home. Her parents were photographer Guillermo Kahlo (1871–1941) and Matilde Calderón y González (1876–1932), who were 36 and 30 when she was born. Guillermo, originally from Germany, moved to Mexico in 1891 after an accident ended his university studies. Kahlo claimed her father was Jewish, but genealogists in 2006 found he was Lutheran. Matilde was born in Oaxaca to an Indigenous father and a Spanish mother. The couple had daughters Matilde (c. 1898–1951), Adriana (c. 1902–1968), and Cristina (c. 1908–1964), and two half-sisters, María Luisa and Margarita, raised in a convent. Kahlo described her childhood as "very, very sad," with both parents often ill and their marriage lacking love. Her relationship with her mother was tense; she described her as kind, active, intelligent, but also calculating, cruel, and fanatically religious. Her father’s photography business declined during the Mexican Revolution due to the loss of government commissions and reduced private clients. At age six, Kahlo contracted polio, which caused her right leg to grow shorter and thinner, leading to isolation and bullying. This experience made her reclusive but also close to her father, who shared her experience of disability. He taught her literature, nature, philosophy, sports, and photography, and encouraged her to pursue strength despite societal norms. Due to polio, she began school later and attended kindergarten and primary school in Coyoacán, then was homeschooled for grades five and six. Her sister Cristina went to a convent school, while Kahlo was enrolled in a German school due to her father’s wishes; she was expelled for disobedience and sent to a vocational teachers’ school, where she was sexually abused by a female teacher. In 1922, she was accepted into the elite National Preparatory School, where she studied natural sciences with the goal of becoming a physician. The school had only 35 female students out of 2,000, and she excelled academically, becoming deeply committed to Mexican culture, political activism, and social justice. The school promoted indigenismo, emphasizing Indigenous heritage and rejecting European superiority. Nine of her classmates, with whom she formed the informal group known as the "Cachuchas," became prominent figures in the Mexican intellectual elite.

A German school due to her father's wishes; she was soon expelled for disobedience and sent to a vocational teachers' school, where her stay was brief because she was sexually abused by a female teacher. In 1922, Kahlo was accepted into the elite National Preparatory School, where she studied natural sciences with the goal of becoming a physician. The school had only recently begun admitting women, with just 35 girls out of 2,000 students. She performed well academically, was a voracious reader, and became deeply immersed in Mexican culture, political activism, and social justice. The school promoted indigenismo, a movement that emphasized Mexico's Indigenous heritage and rejected European colonial superiority. Nine of her schoolmates, with whom she formed an informal group called the "Cachuchas," became leading figures in the Mexican intellectual elite; they were rebellious, staged pranks and plays, and debated philosophy and Russian classics. To conceal her age and to declare herself a "daughter of the revolution," she claimed to have been born on 7 July 1910, the start of the Mexican Revolution, a date she maintained throughout her life. She fell in love with Alejandro Gomez Arias, the group's leader and her first love; her parents disapproved. Due to political instability and violence, they were often separated and exchanged passionate love letters. On 17 September 1925, Kahlo and Arias were on their way home from school when they got off a bus to retrieve an umbrella Kahlo had left behind, then boarded a second crowded bus. The driver attempted to pass an oncoming electric streetcar, which crashed into the wooden bus, dragging it a few feet. Several passengers were killed; Arias suffered minor injuries, but Frida was impaled by an iron handrail through her pelvis. She later described the injury as "the way a sword pierces a bull," and the handrail was removed by Arias and others, causing her immense pain. Kahlo suffered multiple injuries: a fractured pelvic bone, punctured abdomen and uterus, a broken spine in three places, eleven fractures in her right leg, a crushed and dislocated right foot, a broken collarbone, and a dislocated shoulder. She spent a month in hospital and two months recovering at home before returning to work. X-rays revealed that the accident had displaced three vertebrae, and she was required to wear a plaster corset for the better part of three months, confining her to bed rest. The accident ended her dreams of becoming a physician and caused her lifelong pain and illness; her friend Andrés Henestrosa stated that Kahlo "lived dying." By late 1927, her bed rest ended, and she began socializing with her former schoolfriends, who were now university students and involved in student politics. She joined the Mexican Communist Party (PCM) and met political activists and artists such as Julio Antonio Mella and photographer Tina Modotti. At one of Modotti's parties in June 1928, Kahlo was introduced to Diego Rivera. They had met briefly in 1922 when he was painting a mural at her school. Shortly after their 1928 introduction, Kahlo asked Rivera to judge whether her paintings showed enough talent for her to pursue a career as an artist. Rivera recalled being impressed by her work, stating it demonstrated "an unusual energy of expression, precise delineation of character, and true severity... They had a fundamental plastic honesty, and an artistic personality of their own... It was obvious to me that this girl was an authentic artist." Kahlo soon began a relationship with Rivera, who was 21 years her senior and had two common-law wives. They were married in a civil ceremony at the town hall of Coyoacán on 21 August 1929. Her mother opposed the marriage, referring to it as a "marriage between an elephant and a dove," a comment based on Rivera's size and Kahlo's fragility; her father approved, as Rivera was wealthy and could support Kahlo, who could not work and required expensive medical treatment. The wedding was reported by Mexican and international press, and the couple became the subject of constant media attention, referred to simply as "Diego and Frida." In late 1929, Kahlo and Rivera moved to Cuernavaca in Morelos, where Rivera had been commissioned to paint murals for the Palace of Cortés. Around the same time, she resigned from the PCM in support of Rivera, who had been expelled shortly before the marriage for supporting the leftist opposition within the Third International. During the civil war in Morelos, life in Cuernavaca deepened Kahlo's sense of Mexican identity and history. Like many other Mexican women artists and intellectuals, she began wearing traditional Indigenous Mexican peasant clothing to emphasize her mestiza ancestry: long colorful skirts, huipils, rebozos, elaborate headdresses, and jewelry. She especially favored the dress of women from the matriarchal society of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, which represented an authentic Indigenous Mexican cultural heritage in post-revolutionary Mexico. The Tehuana outfit allowed her to express her feminist and anti-colonialist ideals. After Rivera completed the commission in late 1930, he and Kahlo moved to San Francisco, where he painted murals for the Luncheon Club of the San Francisco Stock Exchange and the California School of Fine Arts. The couple was "feted, lionized, and spoiled" by influential collectors and clients. Her long love affair with Hungarian-American photographer Nickolas Muray likely began around this time. Kahlo and Rivera returned to Mexico for the summer of 1931 and traveled to New York in the fall for the opening of Rivera's retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA). In April 1932, they headed to Detroit, where Rivera had been commissioned to paint murals for the Detroit Institute of Arts. By this time, Kahlo had become bolder in her interactions with the press, impressing journalists with her fluency in English and stating on her arrival that she was the greater artist of the two. "Of course he [Rivera] does well for a little boy, but it is I who am the big artist," she said in an interview with the Detroit News in February 1933. The year in Detroit was difficult for Kahlo. Although she enjoyed San Francisco and New York, she disliked aspects of American society, which she viewed as colonialist, and found most Americans "boring." She disliked socializing with capitalists such as Henry and Edsel Ford and was angered that many Detroit hotels refused to accept Jewish guests. In a letter to a friend, she wrote that although she was interested in U.S. industrial development, she felt "a bit of a rage against all the rich guys here, since I have seen thousands of people in the most terrible misery without anything to eat and with no place to sleep, that is what has most impressed me here, it is terrifying to see the rich having parties day and night while thousands and thousands of people are dying of hunger." Kahlo's time in Detroit was also complicated by a pregnancy. Her doctor agreed to perform an abortion, but the medication was ineffective. Kahlo had previously undergone an abortion in her marriage to Rivera and was deeply ambivalent about having a child. After the failed abortion, she reluctantly agreed to continue the pregnancy, but miscarried in July, which caused a serious hemorrhage requiring two weeks in the hospital. Less than three months later, her mother died from complications of surgery in Mexico. Kahlo and Rivera returned to New York in March 1933, as Rivera had been commissioned to paint a mural for the Rockefeller Center. During this time, she worked on only one painting, My Dress Hangs There (1933), and gave further interviews to the American press. In May, Rivera was fired from the Rockefeller Center project and hired to paint a mural for the New Workers School. Although Rivera wanted to stay in the U.S., Kahlo was homesick, and they returned to Mexico soon after the mural's unveiling in December 1933. Back in Mexico City, Kahlo and Rivera moved into a new house in the wealthy neighborhood of San Ángel, commissioned by Juan O'Gorman, a student of Le Corbusier. The house consisted of two sections joined by a bridge; Kahlo's was painted blue and Rivera's pink and white. The bohemian residence became a key meeting place for artists and political activists from Mexico and abroad. Kahlo experienced further health problems—undergoing an appendectomy, two abortions, and the amputation of gangrenous toes—and her marriage to Rivera became strained. He was unhappy to be back in Mexico and blamed Kahlo for their return. Although he had been unfaithful before, he now began an affair with her younger sister Cristina, which deeply hurt Kahlo. After discovering the affair in early 1935, she moved to an apartment in central Mexico City and considered divorcing him. She also had an affair with American artist Isamu Noguchi. Kahlo was reconciled with Rivera and Cristina later in 1935 and moved back to San Ángel. She became a loving aunt to Cristina's children, Isolda and Antonio. Despite the reconciliation, both Rivera and Kahlo continued their infidelities. In 1936, she resumed her political activities, joining the Fourth International and becoming a founding member of a solidarity committee to aid Republicans in the Spanish Civil War. She and Rivera successfully petitioned the Mexican government to grant asylum to Leon Trotsky and offered La Casa Azul as a residence for him and his wife Natalia Sedova. The couple lived there from January 1937 until April 1939, during which time Kahlo and Trotsky became good friends and had a brief affair. Kahlo painted Self-Portrait Dedicated to Leon Trotsky in 1937, including a written inscription to Trotsky in the painting on a letter that her figure holds. After opening an exhibition in Paris, Kahlo sailed back to New York. She was eager to reunite with Muray, but he ended their affair, as he had met another woman he planned to marry. Kahlo returned to Mexico City, where Rivera requested a divorce from her. The exact reasons are unknown, but Rivera stated publicly it was merely a "matter of legal convenience in the style of modern times... there are no sentimental, artistic, or economic reasons." According to their friends, the divorce was mainly due to their mutual infidelities. They were granted a divorce in November 1939, but remained friendly; she continued to manage his finances and correspondence. Following her separation from Rivera, Kahlo moved back to La Casa Azul and, determined to earn her own living, began another productive period as an artist, inspired by her experiences abroad. Encouraged by growing recognition, she moved from using small tin sheets since 1932 to large canvases, which were easier to exhibit. She adopted a more sophisticated technique, limited graphic details, and began producing more quarter-length portraits, which were easier to sell. She painted several of her most famous works during this period, including The Two Fridas (1939), Self-Portrait with Cropped Hair (1940), The Wounded Table (1940), and Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird (1940). Three exhibitions featured her work in 1940: the fourth International Surrealist Exhibition in Mexico City, the Golden Gate International Exposition in San Francisco, and Twenty Centuries of Mexican Art at MoMA in New York. On 21 August 1940, Trotsky was assassinated in Coyoacán, where he had continued to live after leaving La Casa Azul. Kahlo was briefly suspected of involvement, as she knew the murderer, and was arrested and held for two days with her sister Cristina. The following month, Kahlo traveled to San Francisco for medical treatment for back pain and a fungal infection on her hand. Her continuously fragile health had declined since her divorce and worsened due to heavy alcohol consumption. Rivera was also in San Francisco after fleeing Mexico City following Trotsky's murder and accepted a commission. Although Kahlo had a relationship with art dealer Heinz Berggruen during her visit, she and Rivera were reconciled. They remarried in a simple civil ceremony on 8 December 1940. Kahlo and Rivera returned to Mexico soon after. The union was less turbulent than before for its first five years. Both were more independent; while La Casa Azul was their primary residence, Rivera retained the San Ángel house as his studio and second apartment. Both continued having extramarital affairs; Kahlo had affairs with both men and women, with evidence suggesting her male lovers were more important to her than her female lovers. Despite medical treatment in San Francisco, Kahlo's health problems persisted throughout the 1940s. Due to spinal issues, she wore twenty-eight separate supportive corsets, ranging from steel and leather to plaster, between 1940 and 1954. She experienced leg pain, a chronic hand infection, and was treated for syphilis. The death of her father in April 1941 plunged her into depression. Her ill health increasingly confined her to La Casa Azul, which became the center of her world. She enjoyed caring for the house and garden and was accompanied by friends, servants, and pets, including spider monkeys, Xoloitzcuintlis, and parrots. While gaining recognition in her home country, her health continued to decline. By the mid-1940s, her back had worsened to the point that she could no longer sit or stand continuously. In June 1945, she traveled to New York for an operation that fused a bone graft and steel support to her spine to straighten it. The operation was a failure. According to biographer Hayden Herrera, Kahlo sabotaged her recovery by not resting as required and by once physically reopening her wounds in a fit of anger. Her paintings from this period, such as The Broken Column (1944), Without Hope (1945), Tree of Hope, Stand Fast (1946), and The Wounded Deer (1946), reflect her declining health. In 1950, Kahlo spent most of the year in Hospital ABC in Mexico City, where she underwent a new spine bone graft surgery. The surgery caused a difficult infection and required several follow-up procedures. After discharge, she was mostly confined to La Casa Azul, using a wheelchair and crutches to move. During these final years, Kahlo dedicated her time to political causes as her health allowed. She had rejoined the Mexican Communist Party in 1948 and campaigned for peace, such as by collecting signatures for the Stockholm Appeal. Kahlo's right leg was amputated at the knee due to gangrene in August 1953. She became severely depressed and anxious, and her dependence on painkillers escalated. When Rivera began another affair, she attempted suicide by overdose. She wrote in her diary in February 1954, "They amputated my leg six months ago, they have given me centuries of torture and at moments I almost lost my reason. I keep on wanting to kill myself. Diego is what keeps me from it, through my vain idea that."

Frida Kahlo, who lived in Mexico City, underwent a new bone graft surgery on her spine at Hospital ABC, which led to a difficult infection requiring multiple follow-up surgeries. After discharge, she was largely confined to La Casa Azul, using a wheelchair and crutches for mobility. During her final years, she remained active in political causes, rejoining the Mexican Communist Party in 1948 and campaigning for peace, including collecting signatures for the Stockholm Appeal. In August 1953, her right leg was amputated at the knee due to gangrene, leading to severe depression and anxiety, with her reliance on painkillers increasing significantly. When Diego Rivera began another affair, she attempted suicide by overdose. In her diary from February 1954, she wrote, "They amputated my leg six months ago, they have given me centuries of torture and at moments I almost lost my reason. I keep on wanting to kill myself. Diego is what keeps me from it, through my vain idea that he would miss me... But never in my life have I suffered more. I will wait a while." In her last days, she was mostly bedridden with bronchopneumonia but made a public appearance on 2 July 1954, participating with Rivera in a demonstration against the CIA invasion of Guatemala. She anticipated her death, speaking about it to visitors and drawing skeletons and angels in her diary, with the last drawing being a black angel interpreted by biographer Hayden Herrera as the Angel of Death. Her final words were "Espero Alegre la Salida – y Espero no Volver jamás" ("I joyfully await the exit – and I hope never to return – Frida"). The demonstration worsened her illness, and on the night of 12 July 1954, she developed a high fever and extreme pain. At approximately 6 a.m. on 13 July 1954, her nurse found her dead in bed; she was 47 years old. The official cause of death was pulmonary embolism, though no autopsy was performed. Herrera has argued that Kahlo committed suicide, and the nurse reported that Kahlo had taken eleven painkillers that night, exceeding her prescribed maximum of seven. That evening, she had also given Rivera a wedding anniversary gift over a month in advance. On the evening of 13 July, Kahlo's body was taken to the Palacio de Bellas Artes, where it lay in state under a Communist flag. The following day, it was carried to the Panteón Civil de Dolores for an informal funeral attended by friends and family, with hundreds of admirers outside. In accordance with her wishes, she was cremated in a spectacular manner, with legend stating that mourners saw her hair catch fire, her corpse sit up, and her face form a final seductive grin. Rivera, who described her death as "the most tragic day of my life," died in 1957. Kahlo's ashes are displayed in a pre-Columbian urn at La Casa Azul, which opened as a museum in 1958. In the twenty-first century, Frida has become both a commercial icon and a symbol for various groups, including feminists, the LGBTQ community, and Chicanos, with the term "Fridamania" coined to describe her widespread appeal. The Tate Modern considers her "one of the most significant artists of the twentieth century," and art historian Elizabeth Bakewell calls her "one of Mexico's most important twentieth-century figures." Her reputation as an artist developed late in life and grew posthumously, as during her lifetime she was primarily known as Diego Rivera’s wife and an eccentric in the international cultural elite. Recognition increased in the late 1970s due to feminist scholars challenging the exclusion of female and non-Western artists from art history and the Chicano Movement elevating her as an icon. The first two books about Kahlo were published in Mexico in 1976 and 1977 by Teresa del Conde and Raquel Tibol, and in 1977, The Tree of Hope Stands Firm (1944) became the first Kahlo painting sold in an auction, netting $19,000 at Sotheby's. The first two retrospectives of her work were held in 1978, one at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in Mexico City and another at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Chicago. A joint retrospective of her paintings and Tina Modotti’s photographs at the Whitechapel Gallery in London, curated by Peter Wollen and Laura Mulvey, opened in May 1982 and traveled to Sweden, Germany, the United States, and Mexico. The 1983 publication of Hayden Herrera’s biography Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo became an international bestseller. By 1984, Mexico declared her works part of national cultural heritage, prohibiting their export. As a result, her paintings rarely appear in international auctions, and comprehensive retrospectives are rare. Nevertheless, her works have broken records for Latin American art: in 1990, Diego and I was auctioned for $1,430,000, making her the first Latin American artist to exceed one million dollars; in 2006, Roots (1943) sold for $5.6 million; and in 2016, Two Nudes in a Forest (1939) sold for $8 million. Her popularity has led to the term "Fridamania," and she is considered "one of the most instantly recognizable artists," with her image used as frequently as those of Che Guevara or Bob Marley. Her life and art have inspired a wide range of merchandise and fashion. A biopic, Julie Taymor’s Frida, released in 2002, starred Salma Hayek (who co-produced it), grossed $56 million worldwide, and earned six Academy Award nominations, winning for Best Makeup and Best Original Score. The 2017 Disney-Pixar film Coco features a fictionalized Kahlo as a supporting character, voiced by Natalia Cordova-Buckley. Her appeal stems from a fascination with her painful and tragic life story, and she is seen as a symbol of non-conformity and a "cultural minority," simultaneously a victim and a survivor. Scholars note that her popularity is tied to the sharing of pain as a means of finding dignity and hope in modern society. Kirk Varnedoe stated that Kahlo resonates with contemporary sensibilities due to her self-obsession, creation of a personal world, and constant redefinition of identity—qualities shared by artists like Cindy Sherman and Kiki Smith and popular figures like Madonna. However, critics argue that her life has been mythologized, with dramatic elements overshadowing her art and reducing her works to literal depictions of her biography. Stephanie Mencimer notes that Kahlo has been embraced as a symbol for every politically correct cause and that, like a game of telephone, her story has been distorted, omitting uncomfortable details that reveal her complexity and flaws. This elevation of her life over her art diminishes understanding of her historical significance and obscures deeper truths in her work. Critics also warn that by sanitizing her biography, her image is set up for eventual decline, as is typical of women artists. Baddeley compares interest in Kahlo to that in Vincent van Gogh, noting that while Van Gogh is associated with his paintings, Kahlo is recognized through an image of herself—an observation on how male and female artists are perceived. Peter Wollen draws a parallel between Kahlo’s cult following and that of Sylvia Plath, whose complex art has been overshadowed by a simplified focus on her life. Kahlo’s legacy is commemorated through La Casa Azul, opened in 1958 and visited by about 25,000 people monthly, and Casa Roja (Museo Casa Kahlo), which focuses on her family. In 1985, Mexico City dedicated Parque Frida Kahlo in Coyoacán, featuring a bronze statue. In 2001, she became the first Hispanic woman honored with a U.S. postage stamp, and in 2012, she was inducted into the Legacy Walk in Chicago. In 2007 and 2010, commemorations were held on the centenary of her birth and the birthyear she attested to, including the Bank of Mexico releasing a $500-peso note featuring her painting Love's Embrace of the Universe, Earth, (Mexico), I, Diego, and Mr. Xólotl (1949) on the reverse and Diego Rivera on the front. A major retrospective at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in 2007 attracted approximately 75,000 visitors. Her influence extends to various artistic fields: Paul Leduc released a biopic in 1984, and she is the protagonist of novels by Barbara Mujica (2001), Slavenka Drakulic (2008), and Barbara Kingsolver (2009). James Newton released an album titled Suite for Frida Kahlo in 1994, Michael Marra wrote a song titled "Frida Kahlo's Visit to the Taybridge Bar," and in 2017, Monica Brown and John Parra published a children's book, Frida Kahlo and her Animalitos. In 1996 and 2005, the Mexican Cultural Institute in Washington, DC hosted "Homage to Frida Kahlo" exhibitions showcasing global artists’ works inspired by her. Notable artists such as Marina Abramovic, Alana Archer, Gabriela Gonzalez Dellosso, Yasumasa Morimura, Cris Melo, and Rupert Garcia have used or appropriated her imagery. Kahlo has also been the subject of stage performances, including Annabelle Lopez Ochoa’s one-act ballet Broken Wings (2016), with Tamara Rojo as the lead, and a full-length version, Frida, premiered in 2020 by Dutch National Ballet with Maia Makhateli as Kahlo. Three operas have been composed about her: Robert Xavier Rodriguez’s Frida (1991), Kalevi Aho’s Frida y Diego (2014), and Gabriela Lena Frank’s El último sueño de Frida y Diego (2022). She is the main character in plays such as Dolores C. Sendler’s Goodbye, My Friduchita (1999), Robert Lepage and Sophie Faucher’s La Casa Azul (2002), Humberto Robles’ Frida Kahlo: Viva la vida! (2009), and Rita Ortez Provost’s Tree of Hope (2014). In 2018, Mattel released seventeen new Barbie dolls for International Women’s Day, including one of Kahlo, which drew criticism for its slim waist and missing unibrow. In 2014, she was honored in the Rainbow Honor Walk in San Francisco’s Castro neighborhood. In 2018, the San Francisco Board of Supervisors unanimously renamed Phelan Avenue to Frida Kahlo Way, which is located near City College of San Francisco and Archbishop Riordan High School. In 2019, Rafael Blanco painted a temporary mural titled “Frida Kahlo” that won third place at the Reno Mural Festival. Also in 2019, Frida’s “Fantasmones Siniestros” (“Sinister Ghosts”) was burned to ashes, publicizing an Ethereum NFT. Time created 89 covers to celebrate women of the year from 1920 onward, selecting Kahlo for 1938. In 2022, as part of a collaboration with Centre Pompidou, Swatch released a watch based on The Frame.
